claims.text: The target material is a NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 refractory high-entropy alloy containing trace carbon.
Aging at approximately 400 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere followed by controlled cooling will induce nanometric carbide precipitates.
The carbide precipitates will be finely and uniformly dispersed within the BCC matrix and along grain boundaries.
Nanometric carbide precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the precipitates will increase yield strength and mechanical durability.
The precipitates will impede room-temperature creep deformation and lower the creep strain rate.
The precipitates will promote formation of a uniform and more stable passive surface oxide film.
The more stable passive oxide film will improve corrosion resistance.
The treatment is expected to increase yield strength by approximately 20–30% relative to the untreated baseline.
The treatment is expected to reduce room-temperature creep strain rate relative to the untreated baseline.
The treatment is expected to enhance corrosion resistance relative to the untreated baseline.
Before aging, trace carbon is uniformly present in the as-cast or solution-treated alloy without significant precipitation.
Excessive carbide formation may cause embrittlement.
An optimized trace-carbon content can balance carbide precipitation against retention of ductility.
An inert atmosphere is required to avoid oxidation during aging.
The predicted improvements should hold at room temperature under moderate corrosive exposures representative of aerospace fastener service.
Temperature extremes and highly aggressive chemical environments may fall outside the predicted performance envelope.

contradictions.description: The intervention is repeatedly called a two-step aging treatment, but only one aging hold—approximately 400 °C for 1 hour—is specified. Controlled cooling is mentioned in the hypothesis but is not defined as a second aging step and is omitted from the experimental design.
